title: typeof null
answer: "object" — a long-standing quirk of the language.
explanation: `typeof null === 'object'` dates back to the first JavaScript implementation and was kept for compatibility. Check for null with `value === null`.

title: == vs ===
body: What is the difference between `==` and `===`?

options.t: `===` compares without type coercion; `==` converts operands to a common type first

explanation: `0 == ''` and `null == undefined` are true, but `0 === ''` is false. Prefer `===`; `== null` is an accepted idiom for checking both null and undefined.

title: Floating-point comparison
explanation: Numbers are IEEE-754 doubles, and many decimal fractions are not exactly representable. Compare with a tolerance (`Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON`) or use integer cents / decimal libraries for money.

title: var in loops with setTimeout

options.e: That is the output with let.

explanation: `var` is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the **same** `i`, which is 3 when they run. `let` creates a new binding per iteration, printing 0 1 2.

title: What is a closure?
body: Which statement best describes a closure?

options.t: A function that has finished executing
A function bundled with references to the variables of the scope in which it was created, usable after that scope returns
A way to close browser windows

answer: A function plus its captured lexical environment.
explanation: Closures enable data privacy (module pattern), function factories, memoisation and callbacks that remember state. They keep captured variables alive, which can retain memory unintentionally.

title: Temporal dead zone
body: What happens when code reads a `let` variable before its declaration in the same scope?

options.t: It throws a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone)

explanation: `let`, `const` and `class` declarations are hoisted but uninitialised until their declaration runs; access in between throws. `var` is hoisted and initialised to undefined.

title: Microtasks vs macrotasks
explanation: Synchronous code runs first (A, D). Then the microtask queue (promise callbacks) is drained (C) before the next macrotask (the setTimeout callback, B).

title: Promise combinators
body: Which combinator waits for **all** promises and never rejects?

options.e: Rejects as soon as one promise rejects.
Rejects only if all reject, but resolves on the first success.

explanation: `allSettled` resolves with `{status: 'fulfilled', value}` / `{status: 'rejected', reason}` objects for each input — ideal when partial failure is acceptable.

title: Return value of async functions
body: An `async` function executes `return 5`. What does calling it return?
explanation: Async functions always return promises; thrown errors become rejections. Use `await fn()` or `fn().then(...)` to get the value.

title: Arrow functions and this
body: Which statement about arrow functions is true?

options.t: They create their own `this` based on how they are called
They do not have their own `this`; they capture `this` lexically from the enclosing scope
They can be used as constructors with new

explanation: That makes them ideal for callbacks inside methods, but unsuitable as object methods that need the receiver, and they have no `arguments` object or `prototype`.

title: Prototype chain lookup
body: How does JavaScript resolve `obj.method()` when `method` is not an own property of `obj`?

options.t: It walks up the prototype chain (`Object.getPrototypeOf`) until it finds the property or reaches null

explanation: `class` syntax is sugar over prototypes: methods live on `Class.prototype`, shared by all instances. Missing properties resolve to undefined after reaching `Object.prototype`.

title: const objects
body: What does `const` guarantee for `const user = { name: 'Ann' }`?

options.t: The object can never be changed
The binding cannot be reassigned, but the object's properties can still be mutated

answer: No reassignment; mutation is still allowed.
explanation: Use `Object.freeze` for shallow immutability, or immutable update patterns (`{...user, name: 'Bob'}`) as React state requires.

title: Default sort order
explanation: Without a comparator, elements are converted to strings and compared by UTF-16 code units. Use `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)` for numbers. `sort` mutates the array; `toSorted()` returns a new one.

title: Event delegation

options.t: Attaching one listener to a common ancestor and using event bubbling plus event.target to handle events from many children
Dispatching events to a web worker

answer: One listener on a parent handles events bubbling from children.
explanation: It reduces the number of listeners and automatically covers elements added later. Use `event.target.closest('li')` to find the relevant element.

title: Reflow vs repaint
body: Which style change typically triggers **layout (reflow)** rather than only a repaint?
answer: Changing width changes geometry, forcing layout.
explanation: Geometry changes (width, height, margins, font-size, adding DOM nodes) trigger layout, then paint and composite. `transform` and `opacity` can often be handled by the compositor alone, which is why they are preferred for animations.

title: Cookies vs Web Storage
body: Which browser storage mechanism is automatically sent to the server with matching HTTP requests?
explanation: Cookies travel with every matching request (keep them small; use HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite for session cookies). localStorage/sessionStorage are only readable by JavaScript and vulnerable to theft via XSS, so avoid storing tokens there.

title: Debounce vs throttle

options.t: Run the handler at most once every N ms
Delay the handler until N ms have passed without another event

answer: Debounce waits for a pause; throttle limits frequency.
explanation: Debounce suits search-as-you-type (fire after the user stops typing). Throttle suits scroll/resize handlers that should run periodically during continuous events.

title: Explain the event loop
body: Explain how the JavaScript event loop works, including the call stack, the task (macrotask) queue and the microtask queue.
answer: Synchronous code runs on the call stack; when it empties, all microtasks run, then one macrotask, repeating (with rendering between tasks in browsers).
explanation: JavaScript runs on a single thread with a **call stack**. Async APIs (timers, network, DOM events) are handled by the host and queue callbacks when ready. When the stack is empty the event loop: (1) drains the **microtask queue** (promise reactions, `queueMicrotask`, MutationObserver) completely; (2) the browser may render; (3) takes the next **macrotask** (setTimeout, I/O, UI events) and repeats. Long synchronous work blocks rendering and input — split it up or move it to a Web Worker.
reference: The call stack executes synchronous code; asynchronous host APIs enqueue callbacks. When the stack is empty the event loop drains all microtasks (promise callbacks), allows rendering, then processes one macrotask (timers, I/O, events) and repeats. Microtasks run before the next macrotask, so promise callbacks run before setTimeout(0). Blocking the stack freezes the UI.
